what: Colliers is a Canadian-based global real estate services and investment management firm. It brokers property leases and sales, manages buildings, provides engineering and project management, and runs real estate and infrastructure funds through Harrison Street and other managers.
customers: Commercial property owners, occupiers and investors, governments and institutions, and pension funds and other investors in its funds.
money: Leasing, sales brokerage, property management and valuation.
Engineering, design and project management, mostly for public infrastructure.
Fees from real estate, infrastructure and credit funds.
moat: A strong brand and partnership culture: senior leaders own large stakes in their businesses, which keeps talent. Its growing engineering and fund management arms give steadier fees than brokerage.
risks: Debt of $3.2B against $1.6B of equity is high, the result of many acquisitions.
Commercial real estate transactions are cyclical and dropped sharply in 2023.
GAAP earnings are depressed by amortisation of acquired intangibles and payments to minority partners, so the P/E of 63 is not useful.
Office market weakness could hurt leasing and fund performance.
opportunities: Revenue grew from $4.1B in 2021 to $5.6B in 2025, and $6.1B over the last twelve months.
The forward P/E of about 11 on adjusted earnings is low for a firm with this much recurring revenue.
Engineering and investment management are now large and less cyclical.
Nine analysts average a target near $133, well above the price.
watch: Capital markets transaction volume and fundraising in its investment management arm.
view: Colliers’ trailing P/E of 63 says more about accounting than the business. As a serial acquirer it amortises the intangible assets it buys, and a large share of profit goes to the senior partners who own stakes in their units. On the adjusted earnings the company reports, the forward P/E is about 11, which is cheap for a business that has grown revenue from $4.1 billion to $6.1 billion in four years.

That growth has been bought with debt: $3.2 billion against $1.6 billion of equity. The model works when transactions are strong and acquired businesses keep growing, and it gets uncomfortable when commercial property freezes, as it did in 2023.

The question is whether real estate deal activity recovers. The firm has deliberately built engineering and fund management to reduce reliance on brokerage, and that makes the current valuation look too low. I think the discount to CBRE is wider than the balance-sheet risk justifies, but this is a leveraged bet on a property recovery.
bull: Property transactions recover, fund management grows and the discount to CBRE narrows.
bear: Commercial property stays frozen and debt limits further acquisitions.
